items.stem: Which is a non-renewable energy resource?
items.answer: Natural gas
items.markingKey: Fossil fuels and nuclear fuels are non-renewable: they will run out.

items.stem: Describe how electricity is generated in a coal-fired power station, naming the energy stores involved.
items.answer: Coal is burned (chemical store) to heat water into high-pressure steam (thermal store), which turns a turbine (kinetic) connected to a generator producing electricity.
items.markingKey: burn coal → steam [1]; turbine [1]; generator / stores named [1] [3]

items.stem: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power compared with coal.
items.answer: Advantage: no CO₂ produced when operating / much more energy per kg of fuel. Disadvantage: radioactive waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years / risk of accidents.
items.markingKey: advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: A oil-fired power station has an output of 500 MW and an efficiency of 35%. Calculate the power input from the fuel in MW.
items.markingKey: input = 500/0.35 = 1430 MW. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A coal-fired power station has an output of 2000 MW and an efficiency of 38%. Each kilogram of coal releases 30 MJ. Calculate the input power and the mass of coal burned each second.
A country plans a new coal power station. (a) Describe how the station produces electricity. (b) Calculate the power wasted. (c) Explain why this resource is called non-renewable.
items.answer: (a) Burned to boil water; steam drives turbines connected to generators. (b) 1220 MW (c) The fuel cannot be replaced as quickly as it is used; supplies are finite.
items.markingKey: (a) heat → steam [1]; turbine → generator [1] [2] (b) 1220 MW [1] (c) The fuel cannot be replaced as quickly as it is used; supplies are finite [1]

items.stem: In a fossil-fuel power station, what turns the generator?
options: A turbine driven by steam (or hot gas)
items.answer: A turbine driven by steam (or hot gas)
items.markingKey: Burning fuel boils water; steam drives a turbine connected to a generator.

items.stem: Explain why fossil fuels are described as having energy that came originally from the Sun.
items.answer: They formed from plants (and animals that ate plants) that stored energy from sunlight by photosynthesis millions of years ago.
items.markingKey: plants photosynthesised [1]; buried over millions of years [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a gas-fired power station is useful for meeting sudden increases in demand.
items.answer: Gas turbines can be started up and increased in output quickly, unlike coal or nuclear stations.
items.markingKey: fast start-up [1]; meets peaks [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare natural gas and coal as energy resources for generating electricity. Give one similarity and one difference.
items.answer: Similarity: both are non-renewable and used to produce steam that drives turbines (reliable output). Difference: natural gas: CO₂ emissions; finite; coal: releases CO₂ (global warming) and SO₂ (acid rain); finite.
items.markingKey: similarity [1]; difference with specific detail for each [2] [3]

items.stem: A wood pellets-fired power station has an output of 1200 MW and an efficiency of 33%. What is the power input from the fuel in MW?
A wood pellets-fired power station has an output of 500 MW and an efficiency of 33%. Calculate the power input from the fuel in MW.
items.markingKey: input = 500/0.33 = 1520 MW. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A natural gas-fired power station has an output of 1200 MW and an efficiency of 45%. Each kilogram of natural gas releases 55 MJ. Calculate the input power and the mass of natural gas burned each second.

A country plans a new nuclear fission power station. (a) Describe how the station produces electricity. (b) Give one environmental disadvantage. (c) Suggest one reason the government may still choose this resource.
items.answer: (a) Fission of uranium releases thermal energy to make steam for turbines. (b) Radioactive waste. (c) No CO₂ when running.
items.markingKey: (a) heat → steam [1]; turbine → generator [1] [2] (b) Radioactive waste [1] (c) No CO₂ when running [1]

items.stem: A country plans a new natural gas power station. (a) Describe how the station produces electricity. (b) The station outputs 1000 MW at an efficiency of 35%. Calculate the input power. (c) Calculate the power wasted.
items.answer: (a) Burned in gas turbines (or to make steam). (b) 2860 MW (c) 1860 MW
items.markingKey: (a) heat → steam [1]; turbine → generator [1] [2] (b) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 2860 MW with unit [1] [2] (c) 1860 MW [1]

items.stem: In which energy resource is electricity produced like this: plant material or alcohol is burned to make steam for turbines?
items.answer: biofuels
items.markingKey: Biofuels: plant material or alcohol is burned to make steam for turbines.

items.stem: Explain why biofuels are described as "carbon neutral".
items.answer: The plants absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere as they grow, roughly equal to the CO₂ released when the fuel is burned.
items.markingKey: CO₂ absorbed in growth [1]; balances CO₂ released [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a hydroelectric station can respond quickly to a sudden rise in demand.
items.answer: Water stored behind the dam can be released through the turbines almost immediately by opening the gates.
items.markingKey: stored water [1]; released quickly [1] [2]

items.stem: At a hydroelectric dam, 100000 kg of water falls through a height of 50 m every second (g = 9.8 N/kg). Work out the gravitational potential energy lost by the water each second.
items.markingKey: mgΔh = 100000 × 9.8 × 50 = 49 000 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sunlight delivers 1000 W per square metre to solar panels of total area 20 m² with efficiency 20%. (a) Calculate the electrical power output. (b) Calculate the electrical energy produced in 4 hours of such sunshine in MJ.
A town near Nairobi is considering geothermal power. (a) Give two disadvantages. (b) Explain whether it can supply electricity at all times.
items.answer: (a) only in volcanic regions; drilling cost. (b) Yes, it is reliable.
items.markingKey: (a) only in volcanic regions [1]; drilling cost [1] [2] (b) Yes [1]; it is reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Which renewable energy resource does NOT get its energy from the Sun?
items.answer: tidal
items.markingKey: Tidal (Moon’s gravity) and geothermal (hot rocks/radioactive decay inside the Earth) do not come from the Sun.

items.stem: Describe the energy transfers in a wind turbine.
items.answer: Kinetic energy of the moving air is transferred to kinetic energy of the blades and generator, then transferred electrically.
items.markingKey: kinetic of air → blades [1]; generator, electrical [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why geothermal power is only used in a few countries.
items.answer: It needs hot rocks close to the surface, which occur mainly in volcanic regions such as Iceland or Kenya.
items.markingKey: needs hot rocks near surface [1]; volcanic regions [1] [2]

items.stem: At a hydroelectric dam, 10000 kg of water falls through a height of 150 m every second (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the gravitational potential energy lost by the water each second.
items.markingKey: mgΔh = 10000 × 9.8 × 150 = 14 700 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: At a hydroelectric dam, 200000 kg of water falls through a height of 100 m every second (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost by the water each second.
items.markingKey: mgΔh = 200000 × 9.8 × 100 = 196 000 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: At a hydroelectric dam, 100 m³ of water (density 1000 kg/m³) falls 200 m through the turbines every second (g = 9.8 N/kg). The efficiency is 90%. Calculate the electrical power output in MW.
items.answer: 176 MW

items.stem: Sunlight delivers 1000 W per square metre to solar panels of total area 4 m² with efficiency 20%. (a) Calculate the electrical power output. (b) Calculate the electrical energy produced in 5 hours of such sunshine in MJ.
A town near Doha is considering solar-cell power. (a) Describe how electricity is generated using solar cells. (b) Give two advantages.
items.answer: (a) Light is transferred directly to electrical energy in photovoltaic cells. (b) no fuel cost; no emissions when running; good for remote places.
items.markingKey: (a) Light is transferred directly to electrical energy in photovoltaic cells (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) no fuel cost [1]; no emissions when running, good for remote places [1] [2]

items.stem: A town near Seoul is considering tidal power. (a) Describe how electricity is generated using tidal. (b) Give two advantages. (c) Explain whether it can supply electricity at all times.
items.answer: (a) Tidal water flows through turbines in a barrage. (b) predictable; no emissions when running. (c) No: output varies (tides), so backup or storage is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) Tidal water flows through turbines in a barrage (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) predictable [1]; no emissions when running [1] [2] (c) No [1]; output varies (tides), so backup or storage is needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Which energy resource is the least reliable for continuous electricity supply?
items.answer: Wind
items.markingKey: Wind speed varies; no output on calm days.

items.stem: Explain why many countries use a mix of energy resources rather than one.
items.answer: Different resources have different strengths: reliable ones (nuclear, gas, hydro) cover base load and peaks, while renewables cut emissions; a mix protects supply when one is unavailable.
items.markingKey: reliability/backup [1]; reduce emissions/cost balance [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why solar power is more suitable for a country near the equator than for one far from it.
items.answer: Near the equator there is more intense sunlight and more consistent day length all year, so panels produce more energy.
items.markingKey: more intense sunlight [1]; consistent through the year [1] [2]

items.stem: A remote island in the Pacific with strong winds and frequent sunshine needs a new source of electricity. Suggest the most suitable energy resource and justify your choice, including one disadvantage.
items.answer: Wind and solar with battery storage: no fuel needs shipping; both available; storage covers calm/night. Disadvantage, e.g. unreliable (depends on wind).
items.markingKey: sensible choice [1]; justified by local conditions [1]; disadvantage [1] [3]

items.stem: A mountainous country with high rainfall and deep valleys needs a new source of electricity. Suggest the most suitable energy resource and justify your choice, including one disadvantage.
items.answer: Hydroelectric: large reliable supply from stored water. Disadvantage, e.g. flooding of valleys.
items.markingKey: sensible choice [1]; justified by local conditions [1]; disadvantage [1] [3]

items.stem: A government in Riyadh must choose between coal and nuclear fission for a new power station. Evaluate the two options, considering availability, reliability, cost and environmental impact, and give a justified recommendation.
items.answer: Coal: advantages reliable; large output; flexible; disadvantages releases CO₂ (global warming) and SO₂ (acid rain); finite. Nuclear fission: advantages no CO₂ when running; reliable; huge energy from small fuel mass; disadvantages radioactive waste; risk of accidents; expensive to build and decommission. A justified conclusion weighing reliability against emissions and cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each (max 6): availability; reliability; cost; environmental impact; comparison of the two; justified conclusion [6]

items.stem: Which resource has no fuel cost but a very high initial building cost and floods land?
items.answer: Hydroelectric
items.markingKey: Dams are expensive to build and flood valleys.

items.stem: Explain why the cost of electricity from a resource depends on more than just the fuel cost.
items.answer: Building, maintenance, decommissioning and waste disposal costs must be included, as well as how often the station actually runs.
items.markingKey: capital/maintenance [1]; decommissioning/capacity factor [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why geothermal is more reliable than tidal for supplying electricity, and give one reason why a country might still choose tidal.
items.answer: Geothermal can produce electricity whenever needed (reliable); tidal: output peaks only at certain times of day as the tide flows. A country may still choose tidal because predictable.
items.markingKey: reliability of first resource [1]; variability of second with reason [1]; valid reason to choose it [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why natural gas is more reliable than waves for supplying electricity, and give one reason why a country might still choose waves.
items.answer: Natural gas can produce electricity whenever needed (quick start-up); waves: output depends on the weather and sea state. A country may still choose waves because no fuel cost.
items.markingKey: reliability of first resource [1]; variability of second with reason [1]; valid reason to choose it [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how the energy in hydroelectric power originally came from the Sun.
items.answer: The Sun evaporates water, which rises and falls as rain on high ground; the water gains gravitational potential energy that is released through turbines.
items.markingKey: evaporation by Sun [1]; water raised to high ground (GPE) [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
items.answer: Fusion joins light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen → helium); fission splits heavy nuclei (e.g. uranium); both release energy from the nuclear store; fusion powers stars, fission powers nuclear power stations.

items.markingKey: 800 × 10 = 8000 W. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: At a hydroelectric dam, 100000 kg of water falls through a height of 200 m every second (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the gravitational potential energy lost by the water each second.
items.markingKey: mgΔh = 100000 × 9.8 × 200 = 196 000 000 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A town near Doha is considering wave power. (a) Give two advantages. (b) Explain whether it can supply electricity at all times.
items.answer: (a) no fuel cost. (b) No: output varies (weather / daylight), so backup or storage is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) no fuel cost (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) No [1]; output varies (weather / daylight), so backup or storage is needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which resource has no fuel cost but a very high initial building cost and floods land? (b) State two factors to consider when choosing an energy resource for a region.
items.answer: (a) Hydroelectric (b) Any two of: availability, reliability, cost (building and running), environmental impact.
items.markingKey: (a) Dams are expensive to build and flood valleys. (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why geothermal is more reliable than wind for supplying electricity, and give one reason why a country might still choose wind.
items.answer: Geothermal can produce electricity whenever needed (reliable); wind: no output on calm days. A country may still choose wind because no fuel cost or emissions when running.
items.markingKey: reliability of first resource [1]; variability of second with reason [1]; valid reason to choose it [1] [3]

items.stem: Data for four resources (cost of electricity in cents per kWh; reliability; land impact; CO₂ in g per kWh): solar: 6, low, low, 45; nuclear: 11, high, low, 12; coal: 7, high, high, 900; hydroelectric: 8, high, medium, 24. (a) Identify the resource with the lowest CO₂ emissions and the cheapest resource. (b) Evaluate which resource would be best for a country that wants low emissions and a reliable supply.
items.answer: (a) Lowest CO₂: nuclear; cheapest: solar. (b) A reliable low-CO₂ option such as nuclear, hydroelectric is best; renewables need backup when unreliable.
items.markingKey: (a) both identified [2] (b) uses reliability and CO₂ data [1]; justified conclusion [1] [4]

items.stem: Data for four resources (cost of electricity in cents per kWh; reliability; land impact; CO₂ in g per kWh): hydroelectric: 8, high, medium, 24; coal: 7, high, high, 900; solar: 6, low, low, 45; wind (onshore): 5, low, low, 11. (a) Identify the resource with the lowest CO₂ emissions and the cheapest resource. (b) Evaluate which resource would be best for a country that wants low emissions and a reliable supply.
items.answer: (a) Lowest CO₂: wind (onshore); cheapest: wind (onshore). (b) A reliable low-CO₂ option such as hydroelectric is best; renewables need backup when unreliable.

items.stem: A town near Doha is considering hydroelectric power. (a) Describe how electricity is generated using hydroelectric. (b) Give two disadvantages.
items.answer: (a) Water stored behind a dam falls through turbines. (b) flooding of valleys; habitat loss; few suitable sites.
items.markingKey: (a) Water stored behind a dam falls through turbines (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) flooding of valleys [1]; habitat loss, few suitable sites [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why fusion is difficult to use in a power station on Earth. (b) Compare nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
items.answer: (a) Extremely high temperatures and pressures are needed to make nuclei fuse, and it is very hard to contain such hot plasma. (b) Fusion joins light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen → helium); fission splits heavy nuclei (e.g. uranium); both release energy from the nuclear store; fusion powers stars, fission powers nuclear power stations.
items.markingKey: (a) very high temperature/pressure [1]; containment difficult [1] [2] (b) fusion joins [1]; fission splits [1]; where each occurs [1] [3]

items.stem: Trace the energy in hydroelectric back to nuclear fusion in the Sun, describing each stage.
items.answer: Sun evaporates water → rain on high ground (GPE) → falls through turbines.
items.markingKey: fusion in Sun → radiation [1]; intermediate stage(s) [1]; final use [1] [3]

items.stem: Radiation from the Sun delivers 1000 J each second to every square metre of a surface facing it. Work out the energy reaching an area of 5 m² in 300 s.
items.markingKey: 1000 × 5 × 300 = 1.50 × 10⁶ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Almost all of our energy resources depend on the Sun. (a) Name the process that releases energy in the Sun. (b) Name two energy resources that do not depend on the Sun. (c) Explain how the Sun is the source of energy for wind power.
items.answer: (a) Nuclear fusion. (b) Tidal, geothermal (and nuclear fission). (c) Uneven heating of the Earth causes convection currents in the atmosphere.
